```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ldfreq)
has_nsyllable <- requireNamespace("nsyllable", quietly = TRUE)
```

How much of a readability difference comes from sentence length, and how much
from counting syllables? Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level
combine these components. Keeping the counts beside the score lets you inspect
the result before interpreting a difference between texts.

This guide uses **ldfreq 0.3.0.9012 or later**. The helpers in
`examples/readability.R` are explicitly sourced installed examples, not exported
functions. They calculate the published formulas under **recorded counting
conditions**. Automatic syllables use optional **nsyllable >= 1.0.1** and are
estimates; hand-supplied counts need no optional package. These examples do not
establish accuracy on learner writing or validate a reader's ability, a school
placement, or an L2 proficiency level. Only declared English input is supported.

## Start from sentences and inspect what was counted

```{r readability-demo}
demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "readability-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
prepared <- demo$prepared
analysis <- demo$analysis
knitr::kable(prepared$segments[c("document_id", "segment_id", "text", "status")], row.names = FALSE)
```

These short, authored texts expose the arithmetic; they are not a readability
validation sample. Supply one sentence per segment, with unique
`document_id`/`segment_id` pairs and the original text. An empty document still
has a row with `text = ""`. Preserve the original file and the boundary decisions
used to produce these segments. Offsets in the result are local to each supplied
segment, not offsets into an unsupplied file.

```{r own-input, eval=FALSE}
helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "readability.R", package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
prepared <- helper$readability_prepare(segments, language = "en",
  sentence_policy = "reviewed sentence boundaries; headings excluded",
  include = include_sentence)
```

`sentence_policy` describes your procedure; it does not run a sentence splitter.
The helper counts each included segment containing at least one word as one
sentence. It does not silently filter out very short or long sentences. Review
abbreviations, fragments, quotations, lists, colons and semicolons when defining
boundaries. Kincaid and colleagues' [original instructions, pp. 39–40](https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA006655/DTIC_ADA006655.pdf)
include independent units and fragments; punctuation alone is not a complete
boundary rule. `language = "en"` is your declaration, not automatic detection.

The [English tokenizer](english-tokenization.html) retains contractions,
hyphenated words, dotted initialisms and numeric expressions. URLs, email
addresses and punctuation are excluded. Original text and token spans remain
available, including excluded sentences and the tokenizer's URL/email audit.
Curly apostrophes and two Unicode hyphens have canonical token surfaces; their
original surfaces and code-point positions are also saved. No Unicode
normalization or case folding is applied at this stage.

These are operational word rules, **not a reproduction of every original
sampling and counting instruction**. For example, a standalone currency symbol
does not become a spoken word in this tokenizer. [Flesch's 1948 instructions,
reprinted on pp. 106–107](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED506404.pdf) count
hyphenated forms as one word and syllables by pronunciation, including figures
and symbols. They also describe 100-word sampling with a sentence-end adjustment.
Here the ratios use all included text. Audit mismatches before use; if the
operational word units do not fit your protocol, this helper is unsuitable for
that protocol. Do not force its word total to equal a lexical-diversity analysis
with different preprocessing.

## Estimate syllables, then review pronunciations

```{r automatic-syllables, eval=has_nsyllable}
automatic <- helper$readability_score(prepared)
audit <- cbind(prepared$tokens[c("document_id", "segment_id", "original_surface", "counted")],
  automatic$syllables[c("syllables", "method")])
knitr::kable(audit, row.names = FALSE)
```

[nsyllable](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/nsyllable/html/nsyllable.html)
uses a pronunciation dictionary and a vowel-group fallback for unknown words.
The helper distinguishes dictionary matches, fallback estimates and unavailable
counts. A finite estimate is not a verified pronunciation. Digits and dotted
initialisms are withheld for explicit pronunciation review, even if a vowel
guess would return a number. Other abbreviations, names, compounds, misspellings
and pronunciation variants also require review. The result records the package
version, dictionary hash, lowercase policy and estimation method.

Every included word contributes to the word denominator. If even one lacks a
syllable count, both formula scores are `NA`; the known syllable subtotal and
number of unresolved words remain visible. Missing counts are not replaced by
one, and unresolved words are not removed from the denominator.

In the hand-counted example, `1918` and `R.F.D.` initially have no pronunciation
decision. The second analysis supplies four and three syllables respectively,
with the spoken forms recorded in `review_reason`.

```{r review-syllables}
knitr::kable(demo$initial$components, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(subset(demo$reviewed, nzchar(review_reason),
  select = c(token_row, syllables, method, review_reason)), row.names = FALSE)
```

For your own review, copy the **complete** syllable table, edit its counts and
methods, and retain reasons alongside the unchanged first analysis. The
`source_id` and `token_row` keys bind counts to this preparation; tables from a
different source or sentence policy, duplicate keys and missing rows fail.
Rows can be reordered because the keys determine alignment. All source tokens,
including excluded sentences, keep a row; their unresolved counts do not make
included text unavailable.

```{r own-review, eval=FALSE}
reviewed <- automatic$syllables
reviewed$review_reason <- ""
# Change selected syllables, method, and review_reason after inspecting the text.
analysis <- helper$readability_score(prepared, reviewed,
  syllable_source = "pronunciation review; decisions recorded in review_reason")
record <- list(automatic = automatic, analysis = analysis, session = sessionInfo())
```

To supply counts entirely by hand, construct the same four columns:
`source_id` (the preparation's `integrity_sha256`), `token_row`, `syllables`, and
`method`. Counts are positive whole numbers or `NA`, never zero. A descriptive
`syllable_source` is required. Extra review columns are retained. The executable
`readability-demo.R` shows this without requiring nsyllable.

## Check components before interpreting scores

Let W be counted words, S counted sentences and Sy the complete syllable total.

| Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Flesch Reading Ease | 206.835 − 1.015 W/S − 84.6 Sy/W |
| Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level | 0.39 W/S + 11.8 Sy/W − 15.59 |

The first is [Flesch's reading-ease equation](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0057532).
The second is the recalibrated equation in [Kincaid et al. (1975), p. 40](https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA006655/DTIC_ADA006655.pdf).
That recalibration used Navy personnel and training-manual passages; its
[study description](https://stars.library.ucf.edu/istlibrary/56/) does not
establish a universal grade interpretation for L2 writers or readers.

```{r formula-results}
knitr::kable(analysis$results[c("document_id", "measure", "value", "words", "sentences",
  "syllables", "below_word_threshold", "status")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

For `d1`, the two three-word sentences contain six syllables: W = 6, S = 2,
Sy = 6. Reading Ease is **119.190**, and Grade Level is **−2.620**. Values are
not clipped to 0–100 or to nonnegative grades. Neither these values nor a short
text's computable score implies meaningful precision or a reader classification.

`below_word_threshold` defaults to W < 100. This is a configurable **advisory
flag**, not a validated minimum, exclusion rule, or reason to hide a score.
Record your study's sample-length policy separately. Zero words produce
`no_words` and `NA` scores; no artificial sentence or syllable is added.
Document scores use ratios of total counts, not averages of sentence scores.

[quanteda.textstats](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/quanteda.textstats/html/textstat_readability.html)
implements both formulas. With identical component counts, the equations agree.
Its defaults can produce different inputs: hyphens may be split, sentence
length filters apply, and unavailable syllable estimates are replaced by one
in its [implementation](https://github.com/quanteda/quanteda.textstats/blob/master/R/textstat_readability.R).
This helper reuses the optional syllable estimator but exposes missingness and
your supplied boundaries. Agreement on ordinary examples does not establish
end-to-end equivalence for arbitrary texts.

## Keep writer, task and occasion in the research table

```{r readability-study-table}
knitr::kable(demo$study_long[c("observation_id", "writer_id", "task", "occasion",
  "document_id", "measure", "value", "words", "status")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The executable example joins a planned observation roster and a unique
observation/document mapping to the two measures by document ID. The sixth
observation was not submitted; its word count stays `NA`. The submitted empty
fourth document has zero words. These states remain distinct, as do unresolved
syllables in the first analysis. `analysis_id` identifies the saved input,
syllable decisions and settings. Keep one row per observation and selected
measure in a model; do not stack both differently scaled scores as replications.

```{r model-data}
model_data <- subset(demo$study_long,
  measure == "Flesch_Reading_Ease" & status == "ok")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(model_data$observation_id),
  length(unique(model_data$analysis_id)) == 1L)
```

This is an ordinary data frame with writer, task and occasion available to
`lme4`. A hypothetical formula is shown below; the tiny authored dataset is
insufficient to justify fitting it. Specify predictors, coding, random effects
and sample-length exclusions from your research design. The
[repeated-observations guide](repeated-observations.html) demonstrates an actual
model workflow and its diagnostics. This readability table is separate from
the lexical-metric plan contract used there.

```{r model-formula, eval=FALSE}
fit <- lme4::lmer(value ~ task + occasion + (1 | writer_id), data = model_data)
```

## Save enough to return to the text

```{r save-readability, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(demo$record, "readability-record.rds", version = 2)
write.csv(demo$study_long, "readability-study-long.csv", row.names = FALSE, na = "NA")
saved <- readRDS("readability-record.rds")
helper$readability_validate(saved$analysis)
saved$analysis$source$segments
saved$analysis$source$tokens
saved$analysis$syllables
```

The full record retains both analyses, original segments, tokenization audits,
source offsets, counts, decisions, formulas and session information. The hash
check detects changed saved fields; it is not a judgment that the original
sentence or pronunciation decisions were correct. Pin the package revision
and keep the full RDS alongside the CSV. The flat table alone cannot recover
the counting decisions.
